sentences.text: The Moon spins. So why do we only ever see one side of it?
It spins once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to orbit Earth once, about twenty-seven days. NASA calls that synchronous rotation.
Picture a dancer circling a partner, always facing them. The Moon never turns its back to us.
If it didn't spin at all, or spun at any other rate, we'd see different parts of it through the month.
This is called tidal locking, and it's common. All the large moons in our solar system are locked to their planets.
And the far side isn't always dark. It gets sunlight too. At new Moon, the far side is the sunny one.
So, if the Moon keeps staring at us all month... is it keeping an eye on us, or just too shy to turn around?
